text: One inch. Four hundred and forty dollars.
And the one who spotted it... never blinked.
Atlanta airport, 2025. Patrick returned a rental Volkswagen. From Thrifty, a brand owned by Hertz.
The car rolled through an arch. Cameras. Lights. An AI scanner.
Rear wheel. A scuff. About an inch.
The bill: two-fifty for the repair. One twenty-five, processing fee. Sixty-five, admin fee.
Then came an offer. Pay within two days, save fifty-two bucks. Within a week, thirty-two fifty.
Patrick wanted to dispute it. He opened the chat.
It was a bot. It couldn't connect him to a human. It could flag his claim... for later.
So he emailed. A reply could take up to ten days.
Hertz later said a live agent checked the photos and confirmed the damage was new.
But look at that one twenty-five again. Hertz calls it "the cost to detect and estimate the damage."
The scanner found the scuff... and the bill had a line for that, too.
